You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

## task-4bbc870f — translate a marked stencil onto background cells

## Task family: horizontal divider + sparse pattern intersection (task-54cfeb04, unsolved 2026-10-21)

Output 10x11: background 9, mark 3 at (r4,c0), (r5,c1),(r5,c2), (r8,c8). These are exactly the coordinates where both left and right panels contain 9. Thus rule: output 3 iff aligned cells in both panels equal the common foreground 9; else 9.

Demo 2: input 17x4; top 8x4 panel (colors 8/9), separator row 8 of 5, bottom 8x4 panel (colors 9/4). Output 8x4 marks 3 at (r0,c1),(r1,c0),(r2,c1),(r3,c0),(r3,c1),(r4,c2),(r5,c0),(r6,c3),(r7,c0). These also exactly match positions where both panels are 9.

Actual wrong submissions included guesses of 3 at intersection-like positions and various errors, with no per-cell feedback, so they do not disambiguate.

For the solved 25x13 test (field colors 0/9, seed color 5), seed support in its 5x4 bounding box (rows 8–12, cols 6–9) is `[(0,2),(1,1),(2,1),(2,2),(3,0),(3,1),(4,2),(4,3)]`. This yielded two placements: one in the original orientation and one in a reflected/rotated orientation, each repeated at a second vertical offset. More precisely, the union of the two valid support placements produced 16 new 5s; preserve every existing cell, including 9s inside bounding boxes and the seed itself. The submitted grid was confirmed CORRECT.

Demo 1 seed color 1 has bounding-box support rows `[{3,4},{0,2,4},{1},{1}]` (bbox rows 11–14, cols 6–10). Demo 2 and demo 3 also confirm that the stencil may be rotated/reflected when searching. The essential procedure: extract seed support relative to its bounding box; generate/deduplicate all D4 transforms; scan all positions using only cells equal to zero; union all matching support cells; recolor that union with the seed color. ## Task family: task-2f607cd8 (solved 2026-10-21)

Evidence: one demo plus test. The demo has a mostly-0 grid, many isolated color-3 markers, and a distinctive multi-cell source motif near the lower-left. The output replaces each marker with a copy of that motif's colored pattern, leaving the background alone. In this instance, the source motif is at the bottom edge and its continuation/orientation matters; copy its relative pattern at each marker, clipping to grid boundaries.

This task asks to extend a periodic sequence of full-width horizontal rows across the grid. The input may contain blank (all-0) rows followed by repeated solid-color row(s); propagate the observed row-color sequence upward/downward periodically so every row is filled. Preserve the sequence's order and period inferred from the colored rows, cycling through it across the full height. In the solved 5x5 test, input rows were [blank, 9, 4, blank, blank] and output rows were [4, 9, 4, 9, 4], alternating the two observed row colors. Thus row index modulo period determines each entire row's color; fill blanks by periodic continuation. Demo 4 confirmed the general cycle: a 16x16 input with last three rows of colors 1,9,6 became a repeating row sequence 6,1,9,6,... (period 3), anchored so the last row remained 6. Demos 2 and 3 likewise support periodic row completion; some demos use other orientations/periodic diagonal constructions, so identify whether the repeating structure is rows or columns before extending.
